key_insight: The paper provides a systematic benchmark that measures political bias in LLMs by comparing model-generated voting predictions to verified parliamentary roll-call records, revealing consistent partisan alignment patterns across models.
problem_solved: Addresses the lack of objective, reproducible methods and datasets for quantifying political bias in large language models by leveraging real-world parliamentary votes as ground truth for model behavior.
method: Convert parliamentary roll-call items into standardized prompts and collect LLM voting predictions (labels or probabilities).
Align model predictions with verified voting records to compute partisan-alignment metrics (party-level agreement, bias scores, calibration).
Run sensitivity analyses across countries, time periods, and prompt framings to isolate systematic political leanings.
impact: Provides AI practitioners and auditors a scalable, verifiable way to detect and quantify political bias in deployed LLMs, supporting model selection, mitigation strategies, and policy-compliant deployment.
visual_elements: Pipeline flowchart: parliamentary records → prompt construction → LLM predictions → alignment metrics
Heatmap showing agreement rates between models and political parties
Bar chart comparing bias scores or partisan alignment across multiple LLMs
Illustrated example: original vote item, constructed prompt, and model's predicted vote
paper_title: Uncovering Political Bias in Large Language Models using Parliamentary Voting Records
paper_authors: Jieying Chen, Karen de Jong, Andreas Poole, Jan Burakowski, Elena Elderson Nosti
